newsitem.title: UK: NIESR expects slight decline in value of stg.
newsitem.headline: NIESR expects slight decline in value of stg.

text.p: The National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) said it expected a slight decline in the value of sterling.

In a report on the British economy, it rejected suggestions that higher interest rates were needed to prevent a resurgence in inflation, saying the strength of the pound had dampened inflationary pressures which would otherwise have arisen.

The report assumed that official interest rates would rise after Thursday's election to around 6.50 percent by the middle of the year from the present 6.0 percent, but predicted that the increases would be reversed by the beginning of next year.

"It is the high level of the exchange rate that underpins our view of inflation prospects," the NIESR said. "We expect a slight decline in the exchange rate from existing levels in line with interest rate differentials."
"The good short-term prospects for inflation may convince the markets that the longer term outlook is for lower inflation and lower nominal interest rates than they are currently forecasting."
The report said there was evidence that trade prices were being affected by recent exchange rate movements.
"We expect the sterling prices of manufactured and non-manufactured exports to fall by close to three and six percent respectively in 1997," it added.
"This partially offsets the loss to price competitiveness arising from sterling's appreciation but also reduces the profitability of exporting through its effect on business profits."
The report forecast that annual GDP growth would slow to about 2-1/4 percent at the end of the year from 3.0 percent at the start as the contribution to growth of net trade fell off.
This was consistent with growth over the year of about 2-1/2 percent.

"After four years of export-led growth, we expect growth in 1997 to be led by domestic demand, which is forecast to increase by 3-1/4 percent, with consumers' expenditure growing by almost four percent," the NIESR said.
